species.Comments: Widely distributed in a variety of habitats, from the shoreline down to the continental shelf. Juveniles prefer shallow (less than 10-30 m depth) sublittoral waters with complex habitats, such as seagrass beds, areas with gravel, rocks, or boulder, which provide protection from predators (Refs. 89383, 89384). Adults are usually found in deeper, colder waters. During the day, form schools and swim about 30-80 m above the bottom, dispersing at night to feed (Ref. 1371, 89385). Omnivorous; feed at dawn or dusk on invertebrates and fish, including young cod. (Ref. 1371). Migrate between spawning, feeding and overwintering areas, mostly within the boundaries of the respective stocks. Migrations >200 km are rare occurrences (Refs. 89386, 89387). Marketed fresh, dried or salted, smoked and frozen; eaten steamed, fried, broiled, boiled, microwaved and baked (Ref. 9988).

spawning.AddInfos: This stock spawns in colder waters than the other stocks. Cod are rather local in their choice of spawning grounds in the Gulf of Maine, which is the second largest spawning ground in the western Atlantic, especially between Nantucket Shoals and Bay of Fundy. Spawning peaks in February (Ref. 39017).
The most productive spawning ground in the western Atlantic is the eastern half of Georges Bank and the area south of the Grand Banks.

The North Sea is the major spawning area in the eastern Atlantic, generally at depths of less than 50 m and never beyond 200 m.
In the southern part of the range, spawning has been reported to occur in the Southern Bight, Dogger Bank and the English Channel (Ref. 89387).
Up to 19 batches have been observed (Ref. 5946).  Spawning occurs inside the 200 m line (Ref. 3663).
Spawns from Finnmark down to V. Agder (Ref. 118041).
Highest spawning intensity in June.
Peaks in spawning: end of March, end of May and beginning of June and in the last ten-day period in september (Ref.74627).

The time of peak spawning occurred between the end of April and mid June in the 1970s and 1980s. From the early 90s and onwards the time of peak egg production has gradually changed from the end of June tot he end of July (Wieland et al., in press.)
The proportion of spawning males peaked in June and July, while the spawning female proportion peaked in July.
Spawning starts shortly after ice melts and lasts for about three weeks (Ref. 81120).

spawning.AddInfos:
Spawning takes place in deeper water of high salinity. Sex ratio changes with size, season and area and ranges from 41% - 61%. Average dry weight of 100 eggs is 5.7 mg (Ref. 5913). The occurrence of eggs peaks in March and April and larvae are most abundant in May (Ref. 5943) in water of 5-15 °C and 15-17 salinity (pers. comm. A. Müller).
Spawning cumulates in March at depths below 20 m near the bottom. The nursery areas are in the inner coastal zone. Recruitment to the fished stock starts below 2 years and peaks at about 3 years of age (Ref. 5947).

In ICES subdivisions 25-32, the major spawning activities are observed during May to August in the main basins, i.e., Bornholm Basin, Gdansk Deep and Gotland Deep. Nursery areas - as well as summer feeding grounds - are the coastal areas. During winter the stock is concentrating in the main basins either at the ground or above the bottom water, depending on the oxygen conditions (Ref. 5947).

morphdat.AddChars: Protruding upper jaw, a conspicuous barbel on the lower jaw, and light lateral line, curved above the pectoral fins. Predorsal distance is less than one third of total length; body depth about 1/5 of total length. Color varies from brownish to greenish or gray dorsally and on upper sides, becoming pale and silvery ventrally. Peritoneum silvery.

ecology.AddRems:
Opportunistic predator that forages mainly at dawn and dusk (Refs. 1371, 46189). Larvae feed mainly on zooplankton while juveniles prey predominantly on benthic crustaceans; adults feed mainly on zoobenthos and fish (Refs. 5743, 9604, 26813) including juvenile cod. Fish prey becomes more common in the diet with increasing body size (Refs. 1371, 89387). Adults may cover large distances during the feeding period (Ref. 89387). 
Young cod are also preyed upon by different fish species and octopus. Adult cod are prey items of top predators like sharks, rays, whales, dolphins, seals, and sea birds (Refs. 9023, 9581, 26954, 43651, 45735).
In the Baltic it grows up to 5 kg weight in 7-8 years; in the North Sea it reaches 8 kg in the same time span . Natural mortality for adults of both stocks is assumed to be around M=0.2, resulting in a mean adult life expectancy and mean duration of the reproductive phase of 5 years (Ref. 88171).
Parasites of the species include protozoans (trypanosome), myxosporidians, monogeneid,  trematodes, cestodes, nematodes, acanthocephalan, hirudinid and copepods (Ref. 5951).
ecology.AssociationsRemarks: Generally considered a demersal fish although its habitat may become pelagic under certain hydrographic conditions when feeding or spawning.  There is some evidence that  cod leave the bottom and school pelagically to spawn in preferred temperatures when bottom tempetatures are unsuitable.  Gregarious during the day, forming compact schools that swim between 30-80 m above the bottom, and scatter at night  (Ref. 1371). Schooling behavior may be adaptive for feeding.  Reproductive behavior during spawning involves the circling of a female often by only one male per spawning bout (Ref. 86779).
